## Overview

Many plant-disease and pest models are written as rates, not as per-step
probabilities: a susceptible plant becomes infected at rate β times its number
of infected neighbours, and an infected plant is removed at rate γ. Such a
model is a continuous-time Markov chain on the lattice. This vignette shows how
to write one as an `EventRule`, simulate it exactly, event by event, with the
`Gillespie` scheme, act on it at exact times, and run the same rule in discrete
time.

```{julia}
#| output: false
ENV["GKSwstype"] = "100"
using CellularAutomataCore
using Plots
using Random
using Statistics
```

## Rules as rates

An `EventRule`'s function returns the cell's possible transitions as
`rate => new_state` pairs. Here is the contact process (an SIS epidemic):
susceptible cells (0) are infected by each infected neighbour at rate β, and
infected cells (1) recover at rate γ.

```{julia}
sis = EventRule(VonNeumann(1)) do cell, nbrs, ctx
    if cell == 0
        (ctx.p.β * count(==(1), nbrs) => 1,)
    else
        (ctx.p.γ => 0,)
    end
end
```

A problem with an event rule takes real times. `Gillespie()` simulates it
exactly, and `saveat` takes real saving times.

```{julia}
n = 100
u0 = zeros(Int8, n, n)
u0[48:53, 48:53] .= 1
prob = CAProblem(sis, u0, 12.0, (β=2.5, γ=1.0); seed=1)
sol = solve(prob, Gillespie(); saveat=4.0)
sol.t
```

```{julia}
plot([plot(sol; snapshot=i, c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="t = $(sol.t[i])")
      for i in eachindex(sol.t)]...; layout=(1, 4), size=(900, 250))
```

The contact process on the square lattice persists only when β/γ exceeds about
1.65. At 2.5 the infection spreads outwards as a ragged front, and
recoveries leave holes behind it that are soon reinfected.

## One event at a time

A step of a continuous-time integrator is one event: the time jumps to the next
event and exactly one cell changes.

```{julia}
integ = init(prob, Gillespie())
before = copy(integ.u)
step!(integ)
integ.t, findall(integ.u .!= before)
```

## Summaries over time

Saving whole lattices is expensive. A `SavingCallback` records a summary at real
times instead; here the prevalence every 0.1 time units.

```{julia}
prevalence = SavedValues(Float64, Float64)
solve(prob, Gillespie(); callback=SavingCallback((u, t, integ) -> mean(u), prevalence;
                                                 saveat=0.1))
plot(prevalence.t, prevalence.saveval; xlabel="time", ylabel="prevalence", legend=false)
```

## Next-reaction and direct methods

`Gillespie(:next_reaction)`, the default, gives every cell its own exponential
clock in a heap. After an event it recomputes only the cell and its neighbours,
so an event costs the same however large the lattice is. `Gillespie(:direct)`
sums every rate at every event; it is simple and serves as a reference. The two
sample the same process but use their random numbers differently, so they agree
in distribution, not path by path.

```{julia}
function final_prevalences(method; reps=40)
    [mean(final_state(solve(remake(prob; tspan=3.0, seed=s), Gillespie(method))))
     for s in 1:reps]
end
nr, dm = final_prevalences(:next_reaction), final_prevalences(:direct)
(next_reaction=(mean(nr), std(nr)), direct=(mean(dm), std(dm)))
```

```{julia}
small = remake(prob; tspan=3.0)
solve(small, Gillespie(:next_reaction)); solve(small, Gillespie(:direct))
t_nr = @elapsed solve(small, Gillespie(:next_reaction))
t_dm = @elapsed solve(small, Gillespie(:direct))
(next_reaction=t_nr, direct=t_dm, ratio=t_dm / t_nr)
```

The random numbers are counter-based, as everywhere in the package: a cell's
`n`-th waiting time is a function of the seed, the cell and `n` alone. A run
is reproducible and does not depend on the order in which events are
processed.

## Interventions at exact times

Callbacks work as in discrete time. `PresetTimeCallback` and `PeriodicCallback`
also make the simulation stop at exactly their times, even when no event falls
there. Here every infected cell in the left half of the lattice is cleared
(roguing) at t = 6.

```{julia}
rogue! = integ -> (integ.u[:, 1:(n ÷ 2)] .= 0)
s = solve(prob, Gillespie(); saveat=[5.999, 6.0, 12.0],
          callback=PresetTimeCallback([6.0], rogue!))
plot([plot(s; snapshot=i, c=:binary, colorbar=false, title="t = $(s.t[i])")
      for i in 2:4]...; layout=(1, 3), size=(800, 260))
```

Changing the parameters from a callback (`integ.p = ...`) changes every rate
from that moment on. Here transmission falls to a quarter at t = 6, as if a
protectant were sprayed. The prevalence drops at once and then holds roughly
steady. β/γ = 0.625 is below the lattice threshold, so the infection will die
out, but slowly: each cell still has four neighbours to infect, and dense
infected patches persist for a long time before fluctuations clear them.

```{julia}
spray = PresetTimeCallback([6.0], integ -> (integ.p = (β=integ.p.β / 4, γ=integ.p.γ)))
sprayed = SavedValues(Float64, Float64)
solve(prob, Gillespie();
      callback=CallbackSet(spray, SavingCallback((u, t, i) -> mean(u), sprayed; saveat=0.1)))
plot(prevalence.t, prevalence.saveval; label="untreated", xlabel="time",
     ylabel="prevalence")
plot!(sprayed.t, sprayed.saveval; label="sprayed at t = 6")
vline!([6.0]; label=nothing, ls=:dash, c=:grey)
```

## A sparse, seasonal landscape

Real host landscapes are patchy and the weather is seasonal. This model is an
SIR epidemic among plants that occupy 60% of the cells, written with
`@camodel` and an `@events` block. Cells without a host are masked, so they
never change. Infection is driven by a seasonal suitability covariate with
one slice per unit of time. In continuous time the rule sees `ctx.t`, the
integer part of the time, and the rates are recomputed at every whole time.

```{julia}
sir = @camodel PlantSIR begin
    @description "Plant SIR epidemic with seasonal transmission"
    @states state::Int8 = 0 ∈ (0, 1, 2, 3)   # 0 no host, 1 S, 2 I, 3 R
    @parameters β = 1.2 γ = 0.25
    @neighbourhood Moore(1)
    @covariates season
    @events begin
        if cell == 1
            (β * covariate(ctx, :season) * count(==(2), nbrs) => Int8(2),)
        elseif cell == 2
            (γ => Int8(3),)
        else
            ()
        end
    end
end
```

```{julia}
m = 120
hosts = rand(Xoshiro(3), m, m) .< 0.6
start = Int8.(hosts)               # every host susceptible ...
for I in CartesianIndices((58:62, 58:62))
    hosts[I] && (start[I] = 2)     # ... except a small infected patch
end
season = cat([fill(0.5 + 0.5 * cospi(2t / 12), m, m) for t in 0:11]...; dims=3)
plot(0:11, season[1, 1, :]; xlabel="month", ylabel="suitability", legend=false,
     size=(500, 250), marker=:circle)
```

```{julia}
p = CAProblem(sir, (state=start,), 24.0; space=Torus(m, m), mask=hosts,
              covariates=(season=season,), seed=4)
ssol = solve(p, Gillespie(); saveat=6.0)
plot([plot(Torus(m, m), u; c=[:white, :palegreen, :red, :grey40], clims=(0, 3),
           colorbar=false, title="t = $t") for (t, u) in zip(ssol.t[2:end], ssol.u[2:end])]...;
     layout=(1, 4), size=(950, 260))
```

## Ensembles

An `EnsembleProblem` gives every trajectory its own seed, as in discrete time.
Here is the distribution of the final epidemic size in the seasonal landscape.

```{julia}
ens = solve(EnsembleProblem(p; output_func=(s, ctx) -> (count(==(3), final_state(s)), false)),
            Gillespie(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories=40, save_everystep=false)
histogram(ens.u ./ count(hosts); bins=15, xlabel="fraction of hosts removed",
          ylabel="trajectories", legend=false, size=(500, 300))
```

## The same rule in discrete time

An event rule also runs under the synchronous schemes. In each step a cell with
total rate `a` changes with probability `1 - exp(-a)`, and if it changes, it
picks a transition in proportion to the rates. This is the usual chain-binomial
discretisation, and it runs on every backend, GPUs included. It is an
approximation: a cell infected during a step cannot pass the infection on until
the next one, so the discrete-time epidemic lags the exact one. The lag shrinks
as the step shrinks relative to the rates. Below, the rates are divided by `k`
and the run lengthened `k` times, which leaves the exact process unchanged up to
a rescaling of time but makes each step a smaller slice of it.

```{julia}
function prevalence_curve(k; exact)
    q = remake(prob; p=(β=0.2 / k, γ=0.1 / k), tspan=exact ? 100.0k : 100k)
    saved = SavedValues(exact ? Float64 : Int, Float64)
    cb = SavingCallback((u, t, i) -> mean(u), saved; saveat=k)
    exact ? solve(q, Gillespie(); callback=cb) : solve(q; callback=cb, save_everystep=false)
    return saved.t ./ k, saved.saveval
end
plot(prevalence_curve(1; exact=true)...; label="Gillespie (exact)", lw=2,
     xlabel="time", ylabel="prevalence", legend=:topleft)
for k in (1, 2, 4)
    plot!(prevalence_curve(k; exact=false)...; label="Synchronous, rates / $k", ls=:dash)
end
plot!()
```
